newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries close lower as short end suffers Fri.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries close lower as short end suffers Fri.

text.p: U.S. government securities prices closed lower on Friday after a lackluster trading day amid expectations the Fed will tighten monetary policy next week.

The curve flattened further as players moved further out on the maturity spectrum. The bills sector once again took substantial hits. The short end typically is susceptible when the Federal Reserve is viewed as being in a tightening mode.
The Treasury's 30-year bond ended down 4/32 at 95-23/32 to yield 6.97 percent.

Kevin Flanagan, money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc., said there was little if any market reaction to a Johnson-Smick International report saying there was still only a 50-50 chance the Fed would tighten next week.
"I agree only ... that you can't say with 100 percent certainty that the Fed will move next week," Flanagan said. "There's more certainty the Fed will move by Memorial Day,"
The dollar fell after a news wire reported Fed vice chair Alice Rivlin said Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin set limits on his strong dollar policy. The Fed denied Rivlin made the remarks.

The dollar had moved higher Thursday after Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan said central bank policy-makers must be preemptive in battling inflation, comments the markets read as meaning monetary policy would be tightened on Tuesday.

Flanagan said there was some further flattening of the yield curve early in the session, especially in the when-issued two-year note ahead of next week's auction of $17.25 billion of two-years on Tuesday. The current two-year note remained at the same 70-basis-point or so range it had been in while the when-issued was about four basis points flatter most of the afternoon and ended that way.

"We've had a real rise in short-term interest rates, going from (yields) of 5.17 percent on March 11 to 5.40 percent this afternoon. And 23 basis points in the world of short-term interest rates is a big deal," said Hugh Johnson, chief economist at First Albany Corp.
Johnson argued that such a move discounts an increase in the federal funds rate from 5.25 percent to 5.50 percent and a further increase to 5.75 percent.
"This may be the answer to why the stock and bond markets are struggling so. It implies that if the Fed raises rates Tuesday it may not be the last hike," Johnson said.
Short-end yields continued to rise on Friday while the long end remained relatively stable after gaining during the morning.

Portfolio managers are saying "everybody believes this (tightening) is going to work, the Fed is actually going to be successful in slowing the economy," Johnson said. "These guys vote with their money and that's what they're voting."

He said if yields on the 91-day Treasury bill had risen to only to about 5.30 percent, it would have been indicative of expectations the Fed would only tighten once. Fund managers said a near-term rally was possible on a tightening.
Fund managers said the possibility of a rally increased if the Fed issued a calming statement with any tightening, something to the effect that the move was meant as insurance.
Three-month bills closed up six basis points at 5.26 percent; six-month bills were up four basis points at 5.35 percent and year-bill rates ended three basis points higher at 5.53 percent.
Two-year notes ended down 2/32 at 99-08/32, yielding 6.29 percent. Five-year notes closed down 4/32 at 98-14/32, yielding 6.62 percent. Ten-year notes fell 5/32 to 96-13/32, yielding 6.75 percent.
